Between 9 and 18 November, Anthropic, Google and OpenAI released six flagship and mid-tier models between them. Every launch post claimed some benchmark crown, and after a while we stopped being able to tell which of it mattered for us.

So instead of following the launches, we went back to the people who measure this stuff for a living: Epoch AI, METR, Stanford's AI Index team, economists running randomized trials, and Artificial Analysis , which is honestly the site our team opens most often when picking a model. We wanted answers to a few practical questions. How fast are LLMs actually getting cheaper, and why isn't our bill shrinking? What can the models do now that they couldn't a year ago? Who's making money? Does any of it make people more productive? And is it worth running models on our own hardware, rented or bought?

Building a product on LLMs is a bet that prices, capabilities and reliability keep moving in the right direction. The last section is my own guess at how that bet plays out, and it's labelled as such.

## LLMs became "AI" in under four years

ChatGPT launched on 30 November 2022, so it isn't even four years old. In that short time, LLMs have more or less taken over the word "AI". In February 2026 Pew asked 5,119 Americans, for the first time, which technology comes to mind first when they think of AI . 29% named chatbots, either in general or a brand like ChatGPT, and another 6% said generative AI or LLMs. Robots and science fiction got 8%. In the same survey, the share of Americans who had heard "a lot" about AI rose from 26% in 2022 to 48%. ChatGPT alone passed a billion weekly users in August 2026 , and Google's Gemini passed a billion monthly users around the same time.

That matters for this post because the word hides a lot. Speech recognition, computer vision, recommendation systems and plain old machine learning are AI too, and they work under very different economics. We feel this every day. Asya is an AI company, but most of what our developers build are new models that aren't LLMs at all. When someone hears "AI company" and assumes we wrap ChatGPT, it's a good reminder of how much the word has narrowed.

The costs, capabilities and risks we look at here belong to large language models specifically, so in this post we say LLMs when we mean LLMs. The exceptions are proper names (Epoch AI, the AI Index, the EU AI Act) and places where we quote a survey that asked about "AI" in general.

## LLMs are getting cheaper faster than any technology before them

The best long-run data comes from Epoch AI. In September it published The plunging price of thought , which tracks what it costs to hit a fixed score on five benchmarks (GPQA Diamond and FrontierMath among them). Since 2023 that cost has dropped about 47% a quarter, which works out to roughly 13× a year. Epoch compared it with other technologies, and the result is a bit absurd: about 4× faster than the fall in DNA sequencing costs, 6× faster than compute, 18× faster than lithium-ion batteries and 54× faster than electricity between 1892 and 1973.

The top example in the chart is my favourite from the report. GPQA Diamond is a set of PhD-level science questions, and getting 75% of them right went from about 30 cents a question to well under a tenth of a cent in less than 18 months. The bottom example is the one a16z called "LLMflation" back in 2024.

Other studies land in the same place. Mingdeng Du at Wuhan University combined OpenRouter data on 318 models with Epoch's records of 3,237 and found token prices fell about 600-fold, from GPT-3's $60 per million tokens in 2020 to $0.10 for economy-tier models in early 2026. An earlier Epoch study found the rate varies a lot depending on which milestone you pick, anywhere from 9× to 900× a year.

One caveat, which Epoch raises itself : all of this rests on benchmarks. Models can be trained to the test, benchmark questions aren't real work, and the calculation assumes you always switch to the cheapest model that can do the job. Nobody actually does that, so real savings are smaller.

### Market prices roughly halved this year

Actual market prices moved the same way. Axios reported that the Silicon Data LLM Token Expenditure Index, which weights prices by what people actually use, dropped below $1 per million tokens in October. That's down 54% from $2.07 in late May. Ramp's index, built from what businesses really spend on OpenAI and Anthropic, is down 48% from its February peak. Axios puts it down to three things: companies moving spend to cheaper open-weight models, price cuts from the big labs, and agents reusing lots of cached input, which is billed at a fraction of the normal rate.

## So why isn't the bill going down?

Because we use far more tokens. Ramp's data shows that in late 2026 business token usage kept rising while spend stayed flat, two months running. Gartner expects providers' cost of running a trillion-parameter model to fall more than 90% by 2030, but it doesn't think enterprises will see most of that. Its forecast is that total inference spend goes up, since consumption is growing faster than unit prices fall.

Reasoning models are part of it. They think out loud and burn a lot of tokens per answer, which is why Epoch now measures cost per task instead of per token. Artificial Analysis made the same switch: next to its Intelligence Index it now shows cost per task, time per task and output tokens per task, and it treats time per task as its main performance number. That's the view we use day to day, because a model with a low per-token price can still be the expensive option once you count how many tokens it spends thinking.

Agents are the other part. An agent that plans, calls a tool, reads the result and tries again can easily use a hundred times more tokens than a single chat reply. OpenAI says reasoning-token consumption across its enterprise customers is up about 320× year on year.

It's already biting. In McKinsey's 2026 survey , about one in five organisations said "AI-related operating costs" are already limiting how much they use it.

We see it in our own invoices. LLMs can only help so much with the core of our work, and yet the tokens we burn on Cursor and Claude keep climbing month after month.

What we've taken from this: track cost per finished task, and send each task to the cheapest model that handles it well. Cheap models really are cheap now. The top models are still expensive, and agents can run up a bill fast.

## Self-hosting got relatively more expensive

Once you see how good the open-weight models are (more on that below), the obvious question is whether to run them yourself. We expected 2026 to make that easier. It went the other way: token prices fell, and GPU rents went up.

Some numbers. In October an on-demand H100 cost roughly $2–4 an hour on specialist GPU clouds and marketplaces, and about $7–12 at the big hyperscalers, according to Tech Insider's comparison . Blackwell cards cost more: Nebius lists the B200 at $8.50 an hour, and CoreWeave's 8-GPU B200 node comes to about $8.60 per GPU . Peer-to-peer marketplaces go lower still. On Vast.ai , where independent hosts set their own prices, an H100 SXM was listed from $1.73 an hour with a median of $1.93 on 16 November . The trade-off is that reliability depends on whose machine you land on. Buying an H100 outright costs $25,000–35,000 , and that's before the server you put it in.

Rents have been climbing too. SemiAnalysis found one-year H100 contracts rose almost 40% , from $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 in March 2026. H100 rental prices jumped 22% in the month to 7 September, and the Ornn H100 index was at $2.92 an hour on 1 October. Back in January, AWS raised H200 instance prices by 15% , the first GPU price increase there in about twenty years. Even at the Vast.ai median, one H100 running all month comes to roughly $1,400, before you count anyone's time.

Whether self-hosting pays off depends almost entirely on how busy the GPU is. OpenRouter's guide has a simple rule: divide the hourly rent by what a fully loaded hour of the same tokens would cost through an API. The answer is the share of the time the GPU has to be busy before you save money. If it comes out above 100%, the API wins even if the GPU never idles. That ignores engineering time and the headroom you need for traffic spikes, which both make self-hosting look worse.

A Carnegie Mellon paper on arXiv modelled the full cost of ownership. It found you break even within a few months for small models, around two years for medium ones and about five years for large ones. In practice that only works for organisations with steady, high volume. One 2026 worked example was harsher still: compared with a cheap hosted API for the same open model, self-hosting never broke even. The owned GPU's cost per token was higher than the API price even at full load.

Privacy is a weaker argument than it used to be, too. Routers now offer zero-data-retention endpoints and EU-only routing , which covers a lot of compliance requirements without you owning anything.

There are still good reasons to self-host. Small or fine-tuned models that run close to full load (classification, extraction, embeddings, speech pipelines) can come out ahead. So can workloads with hard data-sovereignty or air-gap rules, or latency targets a shared API can't promise. It's also worth doing just to learn how serving works, since it makes you a much better buyer of APIs. A consumer card like the 32 GB RTX 5090 used in the CMU study runs a decent mid-sized model now. For spiky traffic or anything that needs a frontier model, though, the API is almost always cheaper once you count engineering hours.

### How we split it

We run our own GPU servers: two RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q cards, one RTX 5090 and eight RTX 4090s. When a project needs more, we work with partners who give us access to far bigger clusters. You might expect a setup like that to run our LLM workloads too. It mostly doesn't.

We host exactly one LLM ourselves, for clients with the strictest data-processing requirements. Everything else goes to EU-hosted models on Microsoft Azure and Google Vertex AI, which is the EU-routing point above in practice. That keeps our own GPUs free for what they're best at: training new models and running inference on the custom models we build for partners. Those jobs keep the cards busy, and you can't buy them by the token from anyone else. A general-purpose LLM is the opposite case. We can rent one by the token whenever we need it, so tying up our own cards with it rarely makes sense.

## Buying your own hardware got a lot more expensive

If renting doesn't add up, the next idea is usually to buy a box and put it under a desk. Two years ago that was a reasonable plan. Today it costs a lot more, and the reason is memory. Local LLMs need lots of fast memory, and so do the data centres that serve LLMs to everyone else. Data centres may take as much as 70% of all memory produced in 2026 , and DRAM contract prices rose about 90% in the first quarter alone , the biggest quarterly jump on record. Apple, which usually gets to set its own prices, told the Wall Street Journal it had never seen "a component price increase this much, this quickly" .
